intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the GAD1 gene (605363) on chromosome 2q31.

checks.claim: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 (DEE89) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the GAD1 gene.

paragraphs.text: Developmental and epileptic encephalopathy-89 is an autosomal recessive disorder in which seizures begin in the neonatal period or early infancy, often as epileptic spasms or myoclonic seizures, and are accompanied by severe developmental delay and hypotonia. Some patients have variable features outside the central nervous system, including cleft palate, joint contractures, pes equinovarus, omphalocele, skeletal abnormalities and dysmorphic features (Chatron et al., 2020; Neuray et al., 2020).

paragraphs.text: Chatron et al. (2020) reported 11 patients from 6 unrelated consanguineous families of Algerian, Egyptian, Turkish, Iranian and Brazilian origin with a syndromic developmental and epileptic encephalopathy. In all patients, seizures began in the first 2 months of life, mainly as epileptic spasms or myoclonic seizures. Early EEG showed suppression-burst, burst attenuation or hypsarrhythmia. Eight patients had joint contractures and/or pes equinovarus, 7 had cleft palate and 2 had omphalocele. All living patients had profound psychomotor delay, and 4 patients died before 4 years of age.

paragraphs.text: Neuray et al. (2020) reported 6 patients (3 male and 3 female) from 6 unrelated families of Persian, Pakistani, African American, Sudanese, Egyptian and Turkish ancestry. Four of the families were consanguineous. Seizures began between 2 and 6 months of age and were mainly focal motor seizures. Some patients also had epileptic spasms, focal non-motor seizures or bilateral motor seizures. Medication controlled the seizures in 3 patients, and 3 patients had drug-resistant seizures. At seizure onset, EEG showed burst suppression in 2 patients, diffuse slowing with multifocal and generalized sharp waves in 2, and hypsarrhythmia in 2. Brain MRI was normal except in 2 patients: 1 had slight ventricular enlargement and 1 had moderate global atrophy. All patients had severe developmental delay, and most never developed speech or nonverbal communication. Intellectual disability was severe in 5 patients and moderate in 1. Five of the 6 patients had reduced muscle strength or tone. Four could not hold their head up, sit or crawl, and 2 depended on a nasogastric tube because of dysphagia. Four patients had mild facial dysmorphism, and 1 had cleft palate. Other features occurred without a common pattern: hirsutism, kidney stones, urogenital malformations, diastasis recti, reduced head circumference, clinodactyly, short arms, arthrogryposis of the lower limbs, congenital hip dislocation, high myopia and hearing impairment. Metabolic workups were normal. Three of the 6 patients became seizure-free, yet all had severe intellectual disability, so cognitive development did not improve with seizure control. The authors hypothesized that GAD1 variants affect development independently of seizure control.
